2.text: On the whole, vegetable food is much more used by women and children

3.text: than by men. In tales, men living in solitude are always described as hunting

4.text: animals and procuring animal food. A solitary woman is more frequently

5.text: described as gathering herbs and roots, laying in stores of vegetable food,

6.text: and often it is told how she brings up on it several small children.¹
6.note: Footnote reference marker keyed as superscript U+00B9 per keying_spec.md §2.10; confirmed raised in zoom.

7.text: DISHES. — The Chukchee bill of fare is not very varied. Boiled meat
7.note: Run-in heading printed in small capitals; keyed as plain ASCII capitals per keying_spec.md §2.13.

8.text: forms the staple food, and the brisket is considered the best part of the animal.

9.text: The head of the animal is generally eaten first; and the other parts are pre-

10.text: pared in order, going backward along the body. There are a few more

11.text: elaborate dishes. First of all is kiˊvlet, a kind of soup, which is made of
11.resolved: kiˊvlet = k, i, U+02CA stress, v, l, e, t
11.note: Raised mark between i and v defaults to stress U+02CA per keying_spec.md §4/§5.8; confirmed at 2x, not apostrophe.

12.text: blood mixed with fat, chopped guts, and edible roots if on hand. This soup

13.text: is cooked in large quantities at all the principal ceremonials. It is used for

14.text: sacrifices, and eaten by the guests as the chief course of the feast. Another

15.text: dish is made of pounded flesh mixed with fat and roots and boiled with a

16.text: small quantity of water into porridge.

17.text: Pounded meat mixed with fat, and sometimes also with edible roots, is

18.text: boiled in water, and then well kneaded and formed into large round balls,

19.text: which in winter are frozen hard, and form the chief travelling-provisions of

20.text: the Chukchee. A man going alone on an expedition of any kind will take

21.text: along a ball of frozen meat-pudding and a few sticks of frozen marrow. Meat-

22.text: pudding is prepared in quantity for ceremonials of a social character; for

23.text: instance, for weddings. It is the customary present which is interchanged

24.text: between the families of the groom and of the bride.

25.text: The Chukchee women do not care to prepare these dishes for every-day

26.text: consumption, especially because boiled reindeer-meat is, after all, the dish

27.text: best to their liking. Among the Koryak and the Kamchadal, puddings are

28.text: prepared chiefly of roots, stalks of herbs, and berries pounded and mixed with

29.text: oil; but the country of the Chukchee is too poor to yield vegetable food in
29.note: mz/ocr CATMuS draft read 'vield'; raster clearly shows printed 'yield' (confirmed at 2x).

30.text: sufficient quantities. For sacrificial purposes, however, puddings are made of

31.text: pounded leaves and herbs of the plants named, and on these occasions some

32.text: such pudding is eaten by the people.

33.text: The ordinary meals of the Chukchee consist of solid food only. Like
33.note: Small speck above and left of the paragraph-initial 'T' is ink noise, not a character; confirmed at 2x.

34.text: all the other tribes of northeastern Siberia, they drink tea after the meal.

35.text: Broth is taken afterwards as a cold drink, for which purpose it is often

36.text: cooled with slabs of snow. According to reports of former travellers, they

37.text: ate much snow to quench the thirst; but, owing to the introduction of tea,
37.note: Small speck above and left of line-initial 'a' is ink noise, not a character; confirmed at 2x.

38.text: this custom has fallen off to a great extent.

39.text: TEA, TOBACCO, AND OTHER FOODS. — The people of northeastern Siberia
39.note: Run-in heading printed in small capitals; keyed as plain ASCII capitals per keying_spec.md §2.13.

40.text: use compressed “brick tea” almost exclusively, and drink it very strong and
40.note: Both quote marks curly per keying_spec.md §1/§5.6; confirmed at 2x (mz draft had escaped straight quote for the close).

41.text: black, when their supply is sufficient. They have no milk, and practically no

42.text: sugar; nor do they add tallow or rye-meal, as do the people of southern Siberia.
